title: You say you’ve forgiven them.
paragraphs: You say you’ve forgiven them.
But you still rehearse what they did when you’re alone.
You still feel that tightening in your chest when their name comes up.
You still keep a quiet distance… just in case.
So let’s not pretend. You didn’t forgive them. You managed the pain.
And now you’re wondering what nobody wants to say out loud:
Is there a limit to forgiveness?
Because some wounds don’t feel like they deserve it.
Some betrayals feel too calculated.
Too repeated.
Too deep.
And if you’re honest, part of you believes that forgiving too much makes you weak… makes you a fool… makes you a victim all over again.
You’re not alone in that thought.
Even one of Jesus’ own disciples asked the same question.

“Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times.” (Matthew 18:21–22)
Read that again.
Not because people deserve unlimited forgiveness.
But because you needed unlimited mercy.
That’s the part most people don’t realize.
You measure forgiveness based on what they did.
God measures forgiveness based on what you did.
And what you did wasn’t small.
You lied when it benefited you.
You entertained thoughts you’d be ashamed to confess out loud.
You ignored God when it was inconvenient.
You chose sin, knowing exactly what it was.
God saw it.
You knew.
And still—
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you proved loyalty.
While you were still the offender.
This is where everything shifts.
Forgiveness in the Kingdom of God is not about fairness.
It’s about resemblance.
You either reflect the mercy you received…
or you reveal that you never understood it.
Jesus made it painfully clear:
“If you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” (Matthew 6:15)
That verse unsettles people.
It should.
Because it exposes something deeper than your wound.
It exposes your heart.
But here’s where many get confused—and this matters.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened.
It does not mean removing boundaries.
It does not mean trusting someone who continues to harm you.
Forgiveness is not reconciliation.
Forgiveness is release.
It’s you stepping out of the courtroom where you’ve been replaying the case over and over, acting as judge, jury, and executioner.
It’s you surrendering the right to revenge.
“Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God…” (Romans 12:19)
You don’t forgive because they apologized correctly.
You don’t forgive because they changed.
You forgive because Christ forgave you when you hadn’t done either.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And if you’re still resisting, let’s be honest about why.
Because holding on feels powerful.
It feels like control.
It feels like justice is still alive.
But it’s not.
It’s slowly poisoning you.
“See to it that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble…” (Hebrews 12:15)
That root doesn’t just sit quietly.
It spreads.
Into your relationships.
Into your thoughts.
Into how you see people.
Even into how you see God.
You start to believe He’s as unforgiving as you are.
But He’s not.
He’s holy.
And He’s merciful.
And those two meet at the cross.
Jesus didn’t hang there because sin was small.
He hung there because sin was massive.
Including yours.
Including the way you’ve held grudges.
Including the way you’ve replayed offenses instead of releasing them.
Including the way you’ve demanded justice from others while begging for grace from God.
That tension inside you right now—that’s not weakness.
That’s conviction.
And it’s leading you somewhere.
Because there are only two paths in front of you.
You keep holding on, building a case, protecting your pain, becoming harder, colder, more distant… convincing yourself it’s strength.
Or you let it go—not because it’s easy, not because it’s deserved—but because Christ is enough, and His justice is final.
One path keeps you bound to what they did.
The other frees you, even if they never change.
So here’s the moment.
Not dramatic. Not loud.
Just honest.
You know exactly who you haven’t forgiven.
Their name came up the moment you started reading.
God saw it.
You knew.
So say it—not to me, but as a response in your own heart… or even out loud if you have to:
“I release them.”
Not because they earned it.
Because Jesus paid for it.
Stay with it.
Follow this path if you’re serious about not just feeling convicted… but actually changing.
If someone came to your mind while reading this, send this to them. Not to accuse—but because they might be carrying something just as heavy.
And if this exposed something in you, don’t hide it. Say it. Even just one word—“release”—let it be your first step.
Stay close. There’s more truth that will challenge you, correct you, and rebuild you.
